Let \(\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_0,\dots,X_n)\). Since \(E|X_n|<\infty\), \(S_n\) is integrable. For \(n\ge1\),
\[
E[S_{n+1}|\mathcal F_n]=E[\alpha X_{n+1}+X_n|\mathcal F_n]
=\alpha E[X_{n+1}|\mathcal F_n]+X_n
=\alpha(aX_n+bX_{n-1})+X_n.
\]
Thus
\[
E[S_{n+1}|\mathcal F_n]=(\alpha a+1)X_n+\alpha b X_{n-1}.
\]
For \(S_n\) to be a martingale, this must equal \(S_n=\alpha X_n+X_{n-1}\):
\[
(\alpha a+1)X_n+\alpha b X_{n-1}=\alpha X_n+X_{n-1}.
\]
Rearranging,
\[
(1-\alpha b)(X_n-X_{n-1})=0 \quad a.s.
\]
To have this identically from the given conditional mean (without relying on a degenerate relation between \(X_n\) and \(X_{n-1}\)), we need \(1-\alpha b=0\), i.e.
\[
\alpha=\frac1b.
\]
Using \(a+b=1\), this indeed gives
\[
\alpha a+1 = \frac{a}{b}+1=\frac{a+b}{b}=\frac1b=\alpha,
\quad \alpha b=1.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{\alpha=\frac{1}{b}}.
\]
(If \(b=0\), no such \(\alpha\) exists for a non-degenerate sequence; in the degenerate case \(X_n=X_{n-1}\) a.s. every \(\alpha\) works.)

answer_text:
Let \(\mathcal{F}_n=\sigma(X_0,X_1,\ldots,X_n)\). Since the \(X_n\) have finite means, \(S_n=\alpha X_n+X_{n-1}\) is integrable.

For \(n\ge 1\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[S_{n+1}\mid \mathcal{F}_n]
&=\mathbb{E}[\alpha X_{n+1}+X_n\mid \mathcal{F}_n] \\
&=\alpha \mathbb{E}[X_{n+1}\mid \mathcal{F}_n]+X_n \\
&=\alpha(aX_n+bX_{n-1})+X_n \\
&=(\alpha a+1)X_n+\alpha b X_{n-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(S_n\) to be a martingale, we need

\[
(\alpha a+1)X_n+\alpha b X_{n-1}
=
\alpha X_n+X_{n-1}.
\]

Equating coefficients gives

\[
\alpha b=1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\alpha a+1=\alpha.
\]

From \(\alpha b=1\),

\[
\alpha=\frac{1}{b}.
\]

Using \(a+b=1\), the second equation is automatically satisfied:

\[
\alpha a+1=\frac{a}{b}+1=\frac{a+b}{b}=\frac{1}{b}=\alpha.
\]

Thus, in the nondegenerate case where such an \(\alpha\) exists,

\[
\boxed{\alpha=\frac{1}{b}}.
\]
